title: UniSuper backs tech despite bubble concerns
full_text:
UniSuper has rejected suggestions the technology sector is heading for another dot-com style collapse, arguing the biggest listed AI winners remain supported by earnings even as it steers clear of parts of the market it believes have become overheated.
In an investment update to members, chief investment officer John Pearce said concerns over a technology bubble were understandable given the extraordinary gains in AI-related stocks, but he did not believe today’s market resembled previous speculative booms.
“On balance, I don’t think so for a couple of reasons. Firstly, if we look at the valuations of the so-called Magnificent Seven, they’re certainly not in bubble territory to me. As a matter of fact, if you look at the rise in their valuations, it’s pretty much tracked the rise in their profitability and expected profitability.”
Pearce argued the market was rewarding companies with genuine earnings power rather than fuelling the indiscriminate speculation that defined previous bubbles, saying the rise in valuations across the Magnificent Seven had broadly mirrored improvements in profitability.
“On balance, I don’t think so for a couple of reasons. Firstly, if we look at the valuations of the so-called Magnificent Seven, they’re certainly not in bubble territory to me. As a matter of fact, if you look at the rise in their valuations, it’s pretty much tracked the rise in their profitability and expected profitability.”
That confidence did not extend across the entire AI ecosystem. UniSuper has trimmed some technology holdings, taken profits and avoided areas it believes have become overheated, particularly private AI companies and direct investments in data centres.
Pearce said valuations attached to OpenAI and Anthropic were difficult to justify given both businesses continued to lose money.
“To be clear, I’m not suggesting there are no signs of bubbles anywhere, and I am particularly concerned about the valuations I see in some of these private markets, the unlisted assets.”
“I think they look a bit crazy, quite frankly, particularly when you consider that more and more users are moving to the much cheaper Chinese models. So we are avoiding investments in these types of companies.”
Pearce also said UniSuper was avoiding direct investments in data centres, although it remained constructive on technology over the medium term despite expecting continued volatility.
The comments came as UniSuper reported another strong financial year for members, with its flagship Balanced option returning 10.4 per cent for accumulation members and 11.2 per cent for pension members in the 12 months to 30 June.
International Shares was the fund’s best-performing option, returning 17.9 per cent, while Australian Shares returned 4.7 per cent.
Reflecting on the Balanced option’s performance, Pearce said: “I’m pleased to say that this compares quite favourably with our major competitors. And that 11.2 per cent for our pension members—that’s four consecutive years of double-digit returns.”
Although international equities again outperformed domestic shares, Pearce said Australia’s market continued to lag because it lacked the technology exposure driving returns overseas.
“Four out of the last five years, 11 out of the last 13 years—our Australian Shares option has underperformed the International Shares option.”
Comparing Australia’s largest listed companies with their US counterparts over the past decade, Pearce said the divergence reflected the dominance of global technology companies.
“The reality is that Australia doesn’t really have a tech sector to speak of, and as we know, tech is the dominant investment theme of our generation.”
He argued Australian equities still deserved a place in diversified portfolios because they had delivered strong long-term returns, generated higher income and had historically proved more resilient during previous technology downturns, including the dot-com crash and the market correction in 2022.
